library(fpp3)

Residuals diagnostics

Recall that, in time series, the fitted values are defined as one-step-ahead forecasts on the training data.

That is, if \(t\) is a generic point in time and our training data extends from \(t=1\) to \(t=T\):

\[ \text{fitted values: } \ \ \ \ \hat{y}_{t|t-1} \ \ \ \ 1 \leq t \leq T \]

Consequently, the residuals are defined as

\[ \text{residuals: } \ \ \ \ y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1} \ \ \ \ 1 \leq t \leq T \]

In general, for time series models we check four properties of the residuals:

  1. Autocorrelation of the residuals (information left on the residuals).
  2. Zero mean of the residuals (bias of the forecasts).
  3. Constant variance of the residuals (homoscedasticity).
  4. Normal distribution of the residuals.

A separate .pdf file summarizes these conditions. Below a more succinct discussion:

1 and 2 are more relevant when assessing the model. A model that does not satisfy them can be improved. If several of our models satisfy 1 and 2 (a common situation), we need to select among them. We will learn how to do this using tools like information criteria and cross-validation later in the subject.

  • The bias of the residuals (mean deviated from 0) is easy to fix by subtracting the mean of your residuals from your forecasts.

  • Autocorrelation left in the residuals is more difficult to fix. You may need to include autoregressive terms, external regressors, or change the model altogether. We will deal with these topics later in the subject.

3 and 4 are more related to the computation of prediction intervals.

  • Apart from applying transformations (most commonly a Box-Cox transformation), there is usually little you can do to improve the normality and homoskedasticity of your residuals. If this is a problem that cannot be solved with transformations, changing the model may be the best option.

  • There are alternative approaches to computing the prediction intervals. For example, bootstrapping will allow us to produce confidence intervals even in situations where normality is lost, as long as residuals are uncorrelated and homoskedastic.

Please read carefully section 5.4 of the book as well as the pdf uploaded to blackboard.

Some specific models (e.g linear models) will require that we do some additional checks on the residuals. We will see this in due course.

Example 1 - Production of Bricks

bricks <- aus_production |>
  filter_index("1970 Q1" ~ "2004 Q4") |> # Shorthand for filtering data between 1970 and 2004
  select(Bricks)

Note that here we have created more than one model in one fit object. The result is a model table (mable in this library) with two models.

bricks_fit <- bricks |> model(
                                Mean = MEAN(Bricks), # Fit two models at once
                                Nv = NAIVE(Bricks)
                               )

bricks_fit
# A mable: 1 x 2
     Mean      Nv
  <model> <model>
1  <MEAN> <NAIVE>

The code below extracts the fitted values for all the models in the mable (model table). The column .model is used to distinguish between fitted values:

model_vals <- 
  bricks_fit |> 
  augment()

MEAN model

model_vals |> 
  filter(.model == "Mean") |>
  autoplot(Bricks, colour = "gray") +
  geom_line(aes(y=.fitted), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed")

In the mean model, the fitted values are equal to the mean of the training data. So the residuals are:

\[ \text{residuals} = y_t - mean(y_t) \]

The command gg_tsresiduals provides a convenient summary chart to examine briefly the properties of the residuals.

bricks_fit |> 
  select(Mean) |> # Selects the Mean model
  gg_tsresiduals()
# Compute the mean of the residuals
model_vals |> as_tibble() |>
  filter(.model == "Mean") |>
  summarise(mean = mean(.innov, na.rm = TRUE))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
       mean
      <dbl>
1 -4.86e-15

Note that the residuals of the mean model have the same shape as the data itself. The residuals are the time series minus the fitted values. If the fitted values are the mean of the data, then the residuals are the same data but now centered around zero. Recall from the classical decomposition algorithm that removing the mean from a time series centers it around 0.

Hence the mean model is a great example of a model with unbiased residuals (mean = 0) but correlated residuals.

To assess normality we will use a box-plot and a qqplot of the residuals. Note that, in the box-plot I am adding the mean as a red dot to judge if it differs a lot from the mean or not.

mean_vals <- filter(model_vals, .model=="Mean")

# Generate QQ plot
p1 <- ggplot(mean_vals, aes(sample = .innov))
p1 <- p1 + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line()

# Generate box plot
p2 <- ggplot(data = mean_vals, aes(y = .innov)) +
      geom_boxplot(fill="light blue", alpha = 0.7) +
      stat_summary(aes(x=0), fun="mean", colour= "red") # Include the mean

p1 + p2
Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_segment()`).

An additional graph that can be helpful to assess homoskedasticity is a time series of boxplots.

Time Series of boxplots with each box-plot comprising 1 year:

model_vals <- 
  
  model_vals |> 
  
  # Create a new column signalling the year of each observation
  mutate(
    year = year(Quarter),
    year_group = floor((year - 1970) / 2) * 2 + 1970 # Group two consecutive years
  ) 
  
# Create a time series of box-plots with each box-plot containing
# the observations within a year
model_vals |> 
  
  # Select the appropriate model within model vals
  filter(.model == "Mean") |> 
  
  # Depict the ts of box-plots
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = .innov)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle = 90))

Time Series of boxplots with each box-plot comprising 2 years:

model_vals |> 
  
  # Select the appropriate model within model vals
  filter(.model == "Mean") |> 
  
  # Depict the ts of box-plots
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year_group), y = .innov)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle = 90))
  1. The residuals are highly correlated, as the correlogram clearly shows (ACF values outside the dashed bounds)
  • In this case this is clearly related to the simplicity of the model. The residuals look exactly like the time plot, only shifted by the mean of the time series.
  • We are barely using information in the model. To fix this we would need to change the model.

Note in the time plot that the residuals are simply the time series minus its mean, so they have a trend and all the features of the original time series.

  1. The residuals have mean 0 (they are the series shifted by the mean of the series)

  2. Visual inspection of the variance of the residuals across historical data indicates lack of homoscedasticity. There are recession periods (such as 1982 or 1974) where the variation of the series is much higher.

  • NOTE: in case of doubt, best judgement regarding homoskedasticity can be attained combining visual inspection with some form of statistical testing, but in this subject we will only use visual inspection to assess homoskedasticity.
  1. Visual inspection agrees with the hypothesis that the residuals are fairly normal. The histogram seems relatively bell shaped and the distribution adjusts fairly well to the QQ-plot (except on the tails and perhaps a bit in the middle). The boxplot further confirms the relative symmetry of the distribution, showing as well that the mean is close to the median.
  • To formally assess the normality we would need to perform a test, something we will not do for now.

NAIVE model

Recall that the fitted values for the naive model are equal to the first lag of the data:

\[ \text{forecast equation Naive model: } \ \ \hat{y}_{T+h|T} = y_T \]

By setting \(h=1\) (fitted values are one step ahead forecasts) we get:

\[ \text{forecast equation for h=1:} \hat{y}_{T+1|T} = y_T \]

We want the fitted value at \(t\) and the previous equation is a one step ahead forecast at \(T+1\). We thus perform the change of variable \(t=T+1\), which implies that \(T=t-1\)

\[ \text{fitted value at t:} \ \ \ \ \hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_{t-1} \]

The residuals of the Naïve model are therefore:

\[ \text{residuals Naïve model:} \ \ \ \ y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_t - y_{t-1} \]

An important conclusion follows: if the residuals of the Naïve model are uncorrelated (as is desired), the following equation is satisfied:

\[ y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t \]

If this is the case, \(y_t\) follows the equation of a random walk process. That is, the value \(y_t\) is obtained by adding a random shock \(\varepsilon_t\) to the value at the previous point \(y_{t-1}\). We see this by simply solving for \(y_t\) in the previous equation:

\[ y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]

This makes the Naïve model an excellent benchmark for a lot of data, particularly for many stock market assets, where removing the first lag from the series results in uncorrelated data. In many instances, if only prices are considered, a lot of stock market assets turn out to resemble a random walk. This is related to the efficient market hypothesis, which we will discuss later in the course.

In general, if the last value of the data is a good guess for the next value, the Naïve model is a good benchmark.

  1. The residuals are clearly correlated. The remaining spikes at multiples of the seasonal period (4, 8, 12, 16, 20…) indicate that the naïve model has not adequately captured the seasonal pattern in the data.
  2. The innovation residuals mean is close to 0 (0.08). To formally assess if this difference is statistically significant we could perform a t-test. In practical terms, whether this bias is significant or not will depend on our particular application and goal. In any case, we could remove it from the forecasts.
  3. These residuals are more homoscedastic than those of the mean model. The variance of the residuals remains more uniform across the historical data. The crisis in 1974 and 1982-83 could be treated as outliers.
  4. Visually the residuals seem to be normally distributed. The histogram seems symmetric and relatively bell-shaped. The values adjust well in the qq-plot with the exception of the tails. The box-plox confirms the symmetry of the distribution and the closeness of mean and median. To formally assess the normality we would need to perform a test, something we will not do in this subject.

  1. The residuals seem uncorrelated. This may be surprising, but remember that the fitted values of the naïve model are the first lag of the data. This means that the residuals of the naïve model are actually:

\[ \text{residuals of naïve model:} \ \ \ \ y_t - y_{t-1} \]

So, as explained earlier in this notebook, the residuals of the naïve model when applied to stock data are many times white noise, meaning that the data resembles a random walk.

  1. The mean of the residuals is actually close to 1, indicating that there is a bias in the forecasts. The bias might be small compared to the actual price that we are trying to predict, but we could remove it nonetheless.

  2. The variance of the residuals stays much the same across the historical data, apart from one spike around trading day 130-140. Therefore the residuals’ variance can be treated as constant.

  3. The histogram suggests that the distribution is not fully normal, particularly due to the long right tail where a couple of outliers accumulate. We can further inspect this with the QQ plot above, which shows substantial deviation from normality on the right tail. This deviation is driven by a few outliers, and the distribution follows the normal density for the mid-range of the variable. As a result, the normality assumption for the prediction intervals of our forecasts is questionable.

  1. The residuals are highly correlated. The residuals themselves clearly exhibit the same trend as the data. After all, the residuals of the mean model are the difference between the data and the mean of the data.

  2. The mean of the residuals is actually 0. This is a good example of how a very bad model can still be unbiased. A mean of 0 does not mean the residuals are small — it means the positive and negative residuals cancel out.

  3. The residuals seem fairly homoskedastic, except for the outliers mentioned before.

  4. The histogram, qq-plot and box-plot clearly show how the residuals are not normal.

Portmanteau tests for autocorrelation

Checking if each autocorrelation coefficient is within the negligible autocorrelation limits is equivalent to carrying out multiple hypothesis tests, each one with a small probability of giving a false positive. When performing multiple tests, it is likely that at least one will give a false positive. If you are unfamiliar with this phenomenon, see references 4 and 5.

A possible solution is to test whether the first \(l\) autocorrelation coefficients differ much from the expected outcome for a white noise process. A test on multiple ACFs is sometimes called a portmanteau test, from the French word describing a rack carrying several items of clothing.

There are different possible statistics for Portmanteau tests on autocorrelation:

Box-Pierce Statistic:

\[\begin{align*} Q = T \sum_{k=1}^\ell r_k^2, \end{align*}\]
  • \(l\) is the maximum lag being considered
  • \(T\) is the number of observations
  • \(r_k\) is the k-th autocorrelation coefficient

Ljung-Box Statistic

\[\begin{align*} Q^* = T(T+2) \sum_{k=1}^\ell (T-k)^{-1}r_k^2. \end{align*}\]
  • \(l\) is the maximum lag being considered
  • \(T\) is the number of observations
  • \(r_k\) is the k-th autocorrelation coefficient

Main idea behind both tests:

Instead of evaluating each autocorrelation coefficient individually against a boundary value, we seek to generate a metric of the overall amount of autocorrelation of the series. Both the Box-Pierce and Ljung-Box statistic are defined to grow as the amount of autocorrelation in the series grows. This is because the terms within the sum are proportional to \(r_k^2\), achieving two things:

  1. All the terms of the sum are greater than 0. The greater the autocorrelation of the different lags, the greater the statistic.
  2. Very small autocorrelations become much smaller when squared, while medium-to-large autocorrelations remain relevant in the sum. In fact, all autocorrelations shrink when squared, because they are \(\leq 1\), but the smaller the autocorrelation, the more its initial magnitude is reduced. This ensures that very small autocorrelation coefficients do not substantially contribute to the growth of the statistic, while medium-to-large autocorrelation coefficients remain relevant within the sum.

The examples below might seem obvious but are worth giving some thought (this idea of squaring is prevalent in the logic behind many statistics and formulas):

  • \(0.9 * 0.9 = 0.81\) : reduction of 10% of the initial module (\(1 - 0.9 = 0.1\))
  • \(0.7 * 0.7 = 0.49\) : reduction of 30% of the initial module (\(1 - 0.7 = 0.3\))
  • \(0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25\) : reduction of 50% of the initial module (\(1 - 0.5 = 0.5\))
  • \(0.25 * 0.25 = 0.0625\) : reduction of 75% of the initial module (\(1-0.25 = 0.25\))
  • \(0.1 * 0.1 = 0.01\) : reduction of 90% of the initial module (\(1 - 0.1 = 0.9\))

So, summarizing, squaring the autocorrelation coefficients \(r_k\) attains the following:

  1. It renders all terms in the sum of \(Q\) and \(Q*\) (the two statistics we will use) positive
  2. It scales the importance of each autocorrelation coefficient within that sum:
    • If each \(r_k\) is close to 0 (small autocorrelation), then \(Q\) (or \(Q*\)) will be smaller.
    • If some \(r_k\) values are large (positive or negative), then \(Q\) (or \(Q*\)) will be larger.

Suggested values for \(l\):

\(l\) (the number of terms in the sum) is something we need to choose. The following recommendations are to be followed

  • \(l = 10\) for non-seasonal data

  • \(l = 2m\) for seasonal data, where \(m\) is the period of seasonality

  • Caution:

    • The test is not good if \(T/l < 5\). If this is the case, use \(l = T/5\).

Distribution of the statistic:

The most difficult part when creating a hypothesis test is to prove that a given statistic follows a certain distribution. We are not going to do this here.

Instead, we will use the existing result that, under the null Hypothesis that the series under study is white noise, both \(Q\) and \(Q*\) would follow a \(\chi^2\) distribution with \((l-K)\) degrees of freedom, where:

  • \(l\) is the amount of lags considered in the sum of the statistic. Remember the recommendations given in the previous section.
  • \(K\) are the degrees of freedom constrained during the test. Without any constraints, the set of \(l\) autocorrelation coefficients would have \(l\) degrees of freedom, but with \(K\) constraints it has \(l-K\) degrees of freedom.

The adequate value for \(K\) depends strongly on the model type. There is debate in the time series community about the correct value for K for these tests. We are going to follow the recommendations below, taken from reference 3.

  • If we want to test whether some data (and not the residuals of a certain model) is white noise, we will set \(K=0\) for the test. That is because there would be no model imposing constraints on the data.
  • If we are testing any of the benchmark models described in this subject (Mean, Naive, Drift or Seasonal Naive), we will set \(K\) to be equal to the number of parameters of the model. Remember this is obtained using the function tidy(). Accordingly, the degrees of freedom of the statistic would be \(l-K\).
  • For other model types, limited empirical evidence from reference 3 recommends the following:
    • For ARIMA models, use \(K=p+q\) and hence \(l-K=l-p-q\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.
    • For seasonal ARIMA models, use \(K=p+q\) and hence \(l-K=l-p-q\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.
    • For regression with ARIMA errors, use \(K=p+q\) and hence \(l-K=l-p-q\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.
    • For OLS regression, use \(K=0\) and hence \(l\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.
    • For non-seasonal ETS models, use \(K=\text{number of smoothing parameters}\) and \(l-K\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.
    • For seasonal ETS models, use \(K=0\) and hence \(l\) degrees of freedom for the statistic.

Below a summary of \(H_0\) and \(H_1\):

  • \(H_0: r_{ks}\;come\;from\;white\;noise\).
    • In this case \(Q\) and \(Q*\) would follow a \(\chi^2\) distribution with \((l-K)\) degrees of freedom, where \(K\) is the number of parameters in the model.
  • \(H_1: r_{ks}\;do\;not\;come\;from\;white\;noise\)

Interpretation of the test:

The test is a right-tailed test. Under \(H_0\) (residuals are non-correlated), the value of the statistic should be small and we should remain in the “fail to reject” region. If the statistic resulting from our series is too high, we enter the rejection region. Those values of the statistic have very low probability of occurrence if \(H_0\) is true. Thus, we reject \(H_0\) if the statistic is big enough. This corresponds to a p-value sufficiently small to reject the test.

As usual, we set a confidence level \(\alpha\) to maintain the type I error under control. We then compute the statistic and its associated p-value. If its p-value is smaller than alpha, we reject \(H_0\). Otherwise we fail to reject \(H_0\).

Obtaining the Box-Pierce and Ljung-Box statistics:

We will use the function augment() to obtain the residuals and then features() from the fabletools library (loaded along with fpp3) applied to the innovation residuals.

Note the definition of dof and lag, the arguments required for the test in the code below:

  • lag: the number of autocorrelation coefficients to be considered for the test. That is, \(l\) in the previous discussion.
  • dof: degrees of freedom to be constrained during the test, that is, the value of \(K\) in the previous discussion.
fit_dcmp |> augment() |> features(.innov, box_pierce, lag = 24, dof = 1)
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  State              Industry                           .model bp_stat bp_pvalue
  <chr>              <chr>                              <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Northern Territory Clothing, footwear and personal a… decomp    109.  3.12e-13
fit_dcmp |> augment() |> features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 1)
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  State              Industry                           .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>              <chr>                              <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Northern Territory Clothing, footwear and personal a… decomp    113.  7.44e-14

In both cases the p-value is much smaller than 0.05 and even than 0.01, so we can reject \(H_0\) with a 99% confidence level. In other words, the residuals do not come from a white noise series and are therefore correlated.
